scope: Anti-Xeno combat reference knowledge used by the Mongrels Field Manual and Ask the Mongrels.

entries.ruleOfThumb: The four standard combat Interceptors scale from Cyclops to Basilisk to Medusa to Hydra. Orthrus is an exception with different behavior and no hearts.
details: Cyclops, Basilisk, Medusa and Hydra are the standard combat Interceptor progression.
Heart count rises with difficulty: 4, 5, 6 and 8 respectively.
Basilisk is the speed outlier at about 530 m/s; Cyclops, Medusa and Hydra are listed around 450 m/s.
Orthrus is not a normal heart-cycle combat Interceptor and should not be treated as one.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Interceptor combat is a repeating cycle: damage hull to exert a heart, destroy the exposed heart, handle the post-heart phase, then repeat until all hearts are gone.
details: Thargoid hearts drive the Interceptor's extreme hull regeneration, which is why simply pouring damage into the hull is inefficient.
A heart is normally immune until enough hull damage is dealt to exert it.
Once exerted, the glowing heart can be targeted and damaged; after it is destroyed the Interceptor transitions into its next shield/special-attack phase.
After the final heart, finish the remaining hull once the final shield/health state allows.
entries.operations: Think in cycles rather than one long DPS race: exert, break heart, disengage/manage mechanics, re-engage.

entries.ruleOfThumb: To exert a heart, deal damage equal to 20% of the Interceptor's remaining hull. Once exerted, the heart is vulnerable for roughly 45 seconds.
details: The exertion calculation is based on remaining hull, not the Interceptor's original maximum hull.
The heart glows while vulnerable and the Interceptor regenerates hull rapidly during the exertion window.
Accurate heart damage matters more than spraying the body once the heart is exposed.

entries.ruleOfThumb: After the first heart, Interceptor shields decay on their own. AXI's rule of thumb is roughly 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 minutes from Cyclops through Hydra, so do not automatically waste limited AX ammunition on shields.
details: AXI lists about 1:45 for Cyclops, 3:00 Basilisk, 4:00 Medusa and 5:00 Hydra.
The shield appears after heart destruction beginning with the first heart cycle.
Thermal Vent beam use can be productive during this phase because it cools the ship while also helping wear down shields without spending Guardian ammunition.
commonMistakes: Dumping scarce Guardian ammunition into a shield that will decay naturally when time and positioning are available.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Interceptor swarms become dramatically larger with higher variants: 32 / 64 / 96 / 128 Thargons for Cyclops / Basilisk / Medusa / Hydra.
details: An Interceptor deploys a swarm when engaged and can deploy another after a heart is destroyed.
Only one additional swarm can be banked while another remains active.
Remote Release Flak is the standard anti-swarm tool for conventional AX loadouts.
Medusa and Hydra swarms can use more difficult formations, including ring behavior.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Cold orbiting combines low heat with strong lateral/angular movement. Below about 20% effective heat, an Interceptor's main cannon has great difficulty tracking a properly orbiting ship.
details: AXI describes two core conditions: sufficient perpendicular movement relative to the Interceptor and effective ship heat below 20%.
Heatsinks, Thermal Vent beams and Silent Running are common tools for controlling heat.
FA-Off makes it much easier to maintain an attack vector while preserving lateral movement around the Interceptor.
Cold orbiting does not make the ship invulnerable; poor range control, lightning, swarms and special attacks can still punish mistakes.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Do not loiter close to an Interceptor after a heart break. Lightning can heavily damage shields, disrupt modules and kill your momentum, leaving you exposed to the swarm.
details: The lightning attack is primarily a close-range control/punishment mechanic.
AXI's basic guide warns that getting inside roughly 1 km invites the attack and describes the actual strike envelope around 700-800 m.
The hull damage from lightning itself is not the only danger: immobilization and module disruption can allow the swarm or main cannon to pile on.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Treat caustic as a persistent hull-damage emergency. Remove it with a Caustic Sink/Decontamination Limpet, or deliberately heat the ship high enough to burn it off when appropriate.
details: Interceptors begin using caustic missiles after the second heart is destroyed.
AXI documents caustic removal by sustaining ship heat above roughly 180% for several seconds, or reaching around 250% for immediate removal.
Decontamination limpets can remove caustic while also repairing hull, but require limpets and time.
Caustic Sink Launchers automatically absorb caustic contamination and are recommended for many modern AX builds.
entries.watchFor: Intentional overheating can damage modules. Use heat-cleansing only when the ship and situation can tolerate it.

entries.ruleOfThumb: For normal Interceptor shutdown pulses, the standard Shutdown Field Neutralizer is the team-friendly choice: it protects nearby ships within about 3 km while active.
details: The standard SFN counters regular Interceptor shutdown pulses and protects other ships inside its approximately 3 km field.
The Thargoid Pulse Neutralizer protects only the equipped ship, but is also designed for the stronger Maelstrom surge mechanic.
Both consume SYS capacitor while held; put pips into SYS before the pulse reaches you.
The neutralizer must be active when the pulse wave passes the ship.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Heatsinks are core AX combat equipment because Guardian weapons generate heavy heat and cold mechanics are central to avoiding Interceptor cannon fire.
details: AXI treats heatsinks as essential on conventional Guardian-weapon Interceptor builds.
Using a heatsink during Gauss firing helps keep effective heat below the cold-orbit threshold.
Split Gauss firegroups can reduce momentary heat spikes and make sink coverage easier to manage.
Heat management is both defensive and offensive: staying cold improves survivability while allowing repeated weapon cycles.

entries.ruleOfThumb: A completed Xeno Scanner scan exposes Interceptor information and lets you sub-target hearts, making heart management far easier for newer AX pilots and wings.
details: Once a scan is complete, the HUD can show variant/health/heart information and enable heart sub-targeting.
AXI notes that only one CMDR in a wing needs to complete the scan because the scan data is shared with wingmates.
Experienced pilots can visually target hearts without relying on sub-targeting, but the scanner is a major quality-of-life and teaching tool.

quickFacts.label: Wing requirement
quickFacts.value: One completed scan can share data

entries.ruleOfThumb: Shields do not make AX ships immune to hull damage: Interceptor weapons deal phasing damage that bypasses a portion of shields and ignores normal resistance expectations.
details: The main Interceptor weapon can deal damage through shields directly to hull.
This is one reason AX defense planning values hull integrity, module protection and repair capability even on shielded builds.
Do not evaluate an AX shield tank the same way you would evaluate a conventional PvE shield tank.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Control range deliberately: roughly 1-1.5 km is a common Gauss heart-fighting envelope, while opening to 3 km or more after a heart helps avoid special-attack triggers and buys repair/synthesis time.
details: AXI's basic doctrine keeps Gauss attacks around 1-1.5 km for convergence and falloff management.
Getting too close increases lightning risk.
After a heart break, gaining several kilometers of separation creates time for swarm handling, repairs, synthesis and shield recovery.
Exact range choices depend on ship speed, weapon type, swarm state and Interceptor variant.

entries.ruleOfThumb: The Basilisk is the speed outlier among standard Interceptors at about 530 m/s. Slower AX ships need a deliberate escape/reversal plan rather than assuming they can simply boost away.
details: AXI lists Basilisk maximum speed around 530 m/s versus about 450 m/s for the other standard variants.
Cold boost / boost-pass maneuvers exploit the Interceptor's slower direction change rather than trying to win a straight-line drag race.
Distance management is especially important when you need time for repairs, synthesis or swarm work.

quickFacts.label: Key response
quickFacts.value: Use direction change, not just straight-line speed
